unit.title: Consult with clients and diagnose hair and scalp conditions

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Where is the best place to carry out a consultation?
options: At the reception desk while other clients wait
At the basin, while the hair is being washed
Seated at the work station, face to face, in good light
On the phone the day after the service has been finished

questions.stem: Which is an open question that helps the client tell you more?
options: Do you want a trim?
Is your scalp itchy, yes or no?
How do you usually care for your hair at home?
You don't use relaxer, do you?

questions.stem: Why should you face the client, or use the mirror, and look at her while she talks?
options: It shows you are listening and lets you see her face and hair
It lets you check your own hair while she speaks
It stops the client from asking too many questions about the price
It makes the consultation finish faster

questions.stem: During the consultation, Mrs Reid frowns and pulls away when you touch her hairline. What should you do?

Keep it private and store the record card safely
Post it on the salon's social media page

questions.stem: Which layer of the hair gives it most of its strength, stretch and colour?

The medulla
The follicle
The cortex

questions.stem: What does a raised, rough cuticle usually tell you about the hair?

The hair is very oily

questions.stem: What is the anagen stage of hair growth?

The resting stage before the hair falls
The short change-over stage
The stage when the hair turns grey

questions.stem: What happens in the telogen stage?
options: The hair grows at its fastest
The hair changes colour
The follicle makes a new curl pattern
The hair rests and is later shed

questions.stem: A client is worried because she finds some hairs on her comb each day. What should you tell her?

Losing some hairs each day is normal as old hairs are shed

questions.stem: Which best describes tightly coiled (type 4) natural hair?

Straight hair with no bend at all

options: How many hairs grow on the head
How curly the hair is
How thick each single hair is: fine, medium or coarse
How long the hair has grown

questions.stem: What does hair 'density' mean?

How quickly the hair grows each month in hot weather
How many hairs there are on an area of the scalp
How much the hair shrinks when it dries

questions.stem: Why is an incompatibility test done before a chemical service?
options: To find metallic salts or other products that react with the chemical
To check how many hairs fall out each day
To measure the length of the hair
To see whether the client likes the smell

questions.stem: What does a pull test (gently pulling a small bunch of hair) help you check?

Whether hair is coming out more easily than normal
How oily the scalp is
How the client feels about the price of the service today

questions.stem: When do you carry out a skin test before a chemical service?
options: Never, because skin tests are only needed for nail products
Only if the client has had the service before
After the service, to check for burns
Before the service, as the maker's instructions say

questions.stem: What does a strand test show before a relaxer or colour?
options: How the hair will react to the product and the timing
Whether the client's skin is allergic to the product in use
How many hairs the client has
Whether the scalp is too dry

questions.stem: What is fragilitas crinium?
options: Head lice
Grey hair
Split ends
Dandruff

questions.stem: What is trichorrhexis nodosa?
options: Hair that grows in a round, ring pattern on the crown
An infection caused by a fungus
Hair that has turned grey
Small swollen knots along the hair where it breaks

options: Dandruff; use an anti-dandruff shampoo
Alopecia areata; refer the client to a doctor
Split ends; trim the hair
Head lice; comb the hair out well with a fine comb

questions.stem: What is canities?
options: Grey or white hair
Hair loss from tight styles
Oily scalp
Beaded hair

questions.stem: A client often wears tight cornrows and her edges are thinning. Which condition is this a sign of?
options: Alopecia areata
Pityriasis capitis
Monilethrix
Traction alopecia

questions.stem: Why does coily natural hair often look shorter than it really is?
options: It grows more slowly than straight hair
It breaks off at the root every month
The coils shrink up when the hair is dry
It has no cuticle, so it cannot hold its length

questions.stem: A client is growing out a relaxer to wear her natural hair (transitioning). Where is her hair most likely to break?
options: At the very tips of the new growth
Where the natural new growth meets the relaxed hair
Only at the crown, where the hair is always thickest
Inside the follicle

questions.stem: What is pityriasis capitis?
options: Head lice
Dandruff
Ringworm
Impetigo

questions.stem: Which sign points to tinea capitis (ringworm of the scalp)?
options: Fine white flakes all over the scalp and shoulders, with no patches
A shiny, greasy scalp after one day
Round, scaly patches with broken hairs, which may itch
A few grey hairs at the temples

questions.stem: What does impetigo on the scalp or face look like?
options: Small white flakes that brush off easily onto the shoulders
A smooth, round bald patch
Small knots along the hair shaft
Weeping sores that form yellow, honey-coloured crusts

questions.stem: Which scalp condition is NOT infectious, though the client may still need a doctor?
options: Psoriasis
Impetigo
Ringworm
Head lice

questions.stem: What do psoriasis patches on the scalp usually look like?
options: Tiny white eggs stuck to the hair
Small, round bald patches with no skin change
Thick, raised red patches with silvery scales
Yellow crusts that weep and spread

questions.stem: What are nits?
options: Flakes of dry skin
The eggs of head lice, stuck to the hair near the scalp
Small knots in split hair
Small red spots on the scalp caused by very oily skin and sweat

questions.stem: What is seborrhoea?
options: The scalp makes too much oil (sebum)
The hair turns grey early
The scalp has round bald patches
The hair is full of split ends and knots

questions.stem: You find signs of an infectious scalp condition. What should you do?
options: Tell the client exactly what disease she has and sell her a cure
Do the service quickly so others do not notice
Ignore it unless the client mentions it
Stop, explain kindly, suggest she sees a doctor, and disinfect

questions.stem: Why should a stylist not give a firm diagnosis of a disease?
options: Because clients never want to know anything about their scalp
Because it takes too long
Because the client will pay less
Because only a doctor can diagnose medical conditions

questions.stem: Which question helps you find out what may have damaged a client's hair?
options: Which chemical services and heat tools have you used?
What is your favourite colour of clothes?
Do you prefer mornings or evenings?
How many brothers and sisters do you have?

questions.stem: How can some medicines or a recent illness affect the hair?
options: They always make the hair curlier
They can cause hair loss or make the hair weaker
They turn the hair a brighter colour
They have no effect at all on the hair or the scalp

questions.stem: Your tests show the hair has poor elasticity and is very porous. What should you advise?
options: A strong relaxer today to make it smooth and easier to manage
A permanent colour to cover the damage
Conditioning treatments before any chemical service
A tight weave to hide the damage

questions.stem: What should be written on the client's consultation record?
options: Only the price of the service
Her friends' names and phone numbers
Her answers, test results, the hair and scalp findings and the plan
The stylist's opinion of her clothes

questions.stem: Why should the client sign or agree the consultation record?
options: To show she agrees with the plan and gave true answers
So that she cannot come back to the salon
To let the salon charge her twice
Because she needs it later to open an account at the bank

questions.stem: How should you explain a hair problem to a client?
options: In long scientific words so she trusts you
Loudly, so that other clients can learn
Quickly, without giving her time to ask
In plain words, kindly, and in private

questions.stem: After checking a client who has head lice, what should you do with the combs and capes?
options: Use them on the next client straight away
Clean and disinfect them, and wash the capes
Put them back in the drawer and clean them next week
Rinse them in cold water only

questions.stem: How can you tell that hair is porous by looking and feeling?
options: It feels smooth and looks very shiny
It feels rough and dry and soaks up water fast
It feels heavy, greasy and oily at the roots all day
It has no curl pattern at all

questions.stem: What is monilethrix?
options: Split ends
A fungal infection that spreads across the scalp
Hair loss from tight braids
Hair with a beaded look that breaks easily

questions.stem: How can strong sun and sea water affect the hair?
options: They can dry the hair and fade its colour
They make the hair grow twice as fast in summer
They cure dandruff for good
They make the hair oily at the ends

questions.stem: After the consultation, which is the right thing to do?
options: Do any service the client asks for, even if tests show harm
Refuse to explain the reasons for your advice
Agree a suitable plan, price and aftercare with the client
Book the most costly service without asking

essays.stem: Describe how you carry out a hair and scalp consultation, and the communication skills you use.
essays.modelAnswer: I greet the client by name, seat her at the work station and talk face to face, or through the mirror, in good light and away from noise. I start with open questions, such as 'How do you care for your hair at home?' and 'What would you like to change?'. I ask about past chemical services, heat use, styles such as braids or weaves, health, medicines and allergies. I listen without interrupting, nod, and repeat back what she said to check that I understood. I watch her body language, for example if she flinches when I touch a sore area. Then I look at and feel the hair and scalp, and carry out the tests I need. I explain what I find in plain, kind words, without blaming her, and give her time to ask questions. We agree a suitable service, the price and the time, and I write everything on the record card and ask her to agree it.
markingPoints: Suitable setting: seated, face to face, good light, private
Open questions on hair care, chemical history, health and allergies
Active listening: no interrupting, repeating back, watching body language
Examines hair and scalp and does the tests needed
Explains in plain words, agrees the plan and records it

essays.stem: Describe the three layers of the hair shaft, and explain how the cuticle's condition tells you about porosity and damage.
essays.modelAnswer: The cuticle is the outer layer. It is made of overlapping scales, like tiles on a roof, that point towards the ends. It protects the inner layers. The cortex is the middle layer and the largest. It holds the bonds that give hair its strength, stretch and curl, and the melanin that gives it colour. Chemicals such as relaxers and colour work in the cortex. The medulla is the soft centre, which may be missing in fine hair. When the cuticle is healthy, the scales lie flat and close. The hair feels smooth, looks shiny and takes in water slowly, so it has low porosity. When the cuticle is lifted, chipped or worn away by chemicals, heat or rough handling, the hair feels rough, looks dull, tangles easily and soaks up water and products quickly, so it is highly porous. Porous hair takes chemicals faster and unevenly, so it needs conditioning and careful strand testing before any chemical service.
markingPoints: Cuticle: overlapping protective scales
Cortex: strength, stretch, curl and colour; where chemicals work
Medulla: centre, may be missing in fine hair
Flat cuticle: smooth, shiny, low porosity
Lifted or damaged cuticle: rough, porous, takes chemicals faster, needs care and strand tests

essays.stem: Explain the three stages of the hair growth cycle, and say when hair loss is normal and when you should refer the client to a doctor.
essays.modelAnswer: Anagen is the active growing stage. The hair grows from the bulb at the base of the follicle, fed by the dermal papilla, and most hairs on the head are in this stage, which lasts for years. Catagen is a short change-over stage, when the hair stops growing and the bulb shrinks away from the papilla. Telogen is the resting stage. The old hair stays in the follicle for a few months and is then pushed out as a new hair starts to grow. Because each hair is at a different stage, it is normal to lose some hairs every day, on the comb or in the shower. I would refer the client to a doctor if she is losing much more hair than usual, if hair comes out in clumps, if there are bald patches such as alopecia areata, if the scalp is red, scaly or sore, or if the hairline is thinning from tight styles and does not improve.
markingPoints: Anagen: active growth, most hairs, lasts years
Catagen: short change-over stage
Telogen: resting, then shed as new hair grows
Some daily hair loss is normal because hairs are at different stages
Refers for heavy loss, clumps, bald patches, scalp changes or worsening traction loss

essays.stem: Describe four hair tests used during a consultation. For each, say how it is done and what it shows.
essays.modelAnswer: A porosity test shows how easily hair takes in water and products. I hold a few strands and slide my fingers from the ends towards the scalp: smooth hair has low porosity, while rough, catching hair is porous. An elasticity test shows the strength of the cortex. I gently stretch a wet strand: if it stretches and springs back, it is healthy; if it stretches a long way and does not return, or snaps at once, it is weak. A pull test checks for hair loss. I gently pull a small bunch of hair from the scalp: if more than a few hairs come out easily, I note it and may refer. An incompatibility test checks for metallic salts or other products in the hair that would react with a chemical service. It is done on a few cut hairs, using the method the maker or the Centre gives. I also note texture and density by sight and touch, and do skin and strand tests as the maker requires before chemical services.
markingPoints: Porosity test: method and result
Elasticity test: method and result
Pull test: method and result
Incompatibility test: purpose, on cut hair, maker's or Centre's method
Skin and strand tests as the maker requires, or texture and density noted

essays.stem: Explain what you look for when you analyse natural, textured hair, including a client who is transitioning from relaxed hair.
essays.modelAnswer: I first ask how she cares for her hair, what styles she wears and how often, and whether she uses heat. I look at the curl pattern, from loose waves to tight coils and zig-zags, which may differ across the head. I check the texture and density, and the shrinkage, so that I can judge the true length by gently stretching a coil. Coily hair is often dry, because scalp oil does not travel easily down the coils, so I check the porosity, especially at the ends, and the elasticity. I look closely at the hairline and edges for thinning or broken hairs from tight braids, cornrows or weaves, which may be a sign of traction alopecia. I check the scalp under braids for build-up, flakes or soreness. For a transitioning client, I find the line where the natural new growth meets the relaxed ends. This line is weak and breaks easily, so I advise gentle handling, moisture and regular trims, and record what I find.
markingPoints: Asks about care routine, styles and heat
Notes curl pattern, texture, density and shrinkage
Checks porosity and elasticity, especially the ends
Checks edges and scalp for traction damage, build-up or soreness
For transitioning: finds the weak line of demarcation and advises gentle care

essays.stem: Describe three infectious hair or scalp conditions, the signs of each, and what the salon must do.
essays.modelAnswer: Head lice (pediculosis capitis) are small insects that live on the scalp and lay eggs, called nits, that stick firmly to the hair near the scalp, often behind the ears and at the nape. The scalp may itch. Ringworm (tinea capitis) is a fungal infection that shows as round, scaly, itchy patches, often with broken hairs. Impetigo is a bacterial infection with weeping sores that dry into yellow, honey-coloured crusts. Folliculitis shows as small, red, pus-filled spots around the follicles. All of these can spread to other people. If I see signs of one, I do not carry out the service. I explain kindly and privately what I have seen, without naming it as a firm diagnosis, and suggest she sees a doctor or pharmacist. I record it on the record card. Then I clean and disinfect all the tools and surfaces I used, wash the gown and towels, and wash my hands before the next client.
markingPoints: First condition named with correct signs
Second condition named with correct signs
Third condition named with correct signs
No service; explains kindly and privately, does not diagnose, refers
Records it, cleans and disinfects tools and surfaces, washes linen and hands

essays.stem: Describe four non-infectious hair or scalp conditions, the signs of each, and what the salon can do.
essays.modelAnswer: Dandruff (pityriasis capitis) shows as small white flakes on the scalp and shoulders. The salon can recommend an anti-dandruff shampoo and treatment used as the maker says. Seborrhoea is an oily scalp, where the hair becomes greasy soon after washing. The salon can suggest a gentle, balancing shampoo and light massage only. Split ends (fragilitas crinium) are hair ends that split into two or more parts; they are removed by trimming and prevented with conditioning and less heat. Trichorrhexis nodosa shows as small swollen knots along the hair where it breaks, often from harsh chemicals, heat or rough brushing; the salon can cut off the damage, give conditioning treatments and avoid chemicals until it improves. Psoriasis shows as thick, raised red patches with silvery scales. It is not infectious, but if it is sore or broken the client should see a doctor, and chemicals must not be used over it. These conditions do not spread, but I always record them and refer if the scalp is sore.
markingPoints: First condition with signs and salon action
Second condition with signs and salon action
Third condition with signs and salon action
Fourth condition with signs and salon action
Knows they do not spread, but records them and refers when the scalp is sore or broken

essays.stem: Explain the things in a client's life and hair care that can affect the condition of her hair and scalp.
essays.modelAnswer: General health has a big effect. A poor diet without enough protein, iron and water, illness, a high fever, stress, pregnancy, changes in hormones and some medicines can make hair thin, weak or fall out. Hair care is also important. Relaxers, colour and other chemical services, especially if they are overlapped or done too often, can weaken the cortex and make hair porous. High heat from flat irons, hot combs and blow-dryers dries the hair and causes breakage. Tight braids, cornrows, weaves and ponytails can pull out hair at the edges and cause traction alopecia. Rough combing, harsh shampoos, product build-up and not moisturising can all damage the hair. In Jamaica, strong sun and sea water dry the hair and fade its colour, and chlorine in pools does the same. A good consultation finds these factors, so that I can choose the right service and give helpful advice.
markingPoints: Health factors: diet, illness, stress, hormones, medicines
Chemical services and overlapping weaken the hair
Heat tools cause dryness and breakage
Tight styles cause traction damage; rough handling and build-up
Sun, sea water and chlorine; links to choosing services and advice

essays.stem: Explain how to tell a client that she should see a doctor about a hair or scalp problem, and why confidentiality matters.
essays.modelAnswer: First I make sure we are in a private place where others cannot hear. I speak calmly, kindly and in plain words. I tell her what I can see, for example 'I can see some round patches where the hair has broken', without naming a disease as a firm diagnosis, because only a doctor can diagnose. I explain that it is not safe to do the service today, and why: it could make the problem worse, or spread to other people. I suggest she sees a doctor or pharmacist, and I offer to rebook when the problem has cleared, with a note from the doctor if the Centre's rules ask for one. I let her ask questions and do not make her feel ashamed. I record what I saw and the advice I gave on the record card. Confidentiality matters because health details are private. Sharing them could embarrass the client, break her trust and harm the salon's name, so records are stored safely and only staff who need them may see them.
markingPoints: Private place, calm and kind manner, plain words
Describes what is seen without a firm diagnosis
Explains why the service cannot go ahead and suggests a doctor or pharmacist
Offers to rebook and records the advice
Explains why confidentiality matters and how records are kept safe

essays.stem: Explain what should go on a consultation record card and why the record is important to the client, the stylist and the salon.
essays.modelAnswer: The record card should hold the client's name and contact details, the date, and her answers about health, allergies, medicines and past chemical services. It should list the hair and scalp findings: hair type, texture, density, porosity, elasticity, curl pattern and any conditions. It records the test results, such as skin, strand, pull and incompatibility tests, with dates. It sets out the agreed service, products, timings and price, any contraindications or referral, and the aftercare advice given. The client signs or agrees it. For the client, the record means her needs and any allergies are known, so services are safe and suited to her. For the stylist, it shows what was done before and how the hair reacted, so the next service can be planned, even by another stylist. For the salon, it is evidence that tests were done and advice was given, which helps if there is a complaint or a reaction. Records are kept up to date and stored confidentially.
markingPoints: Personal details, health, allergies and chemical history
Hair and scalp findings and test results with dates
Agreed service, products, price, referrals and aftercare
Client agreement or signature
Why it matters to client, stylist and salon; kept confidential

practical1.title: Full hair and scalp consultation and analysis on a partner, with record card
practical1.brief: Work in pairs inside your group (one group of three if needed), in the Centre's salon, on members who agree to be clients. Try to include at least one member or a training head with natural, textured hair. Each member carries out a full consultation with a partner: seat the client, use open questions about hair care, chemical history, heat, styles, health, medicines and allergies, and listen and repeat back. Then look at and feel the hair and scalp in good light, section by section, and carry out porosity, elasticity and pull tests, and note texture, density, curl pattern and the condition of the edges and scalp. Decide whether there are any contraindications. Fill in a record card and agree a suitable service plan and aftercare with the client. Swap roles. Photos show only hair, scalp and the record cards, never faces.
materials: Wide-tooth combs, sectioning clips and a spray bottle of water
Good lighting or a magnifying lamp
Training head with natural textured hair, if needed
photos: The consultation area set up, with tools and record cards ready
The hair parted in sections to check the scalp
A porosity test being done on a strand
An elasticity test on a wet strand
The hairline and edges being checked
The completed record cards, laid out together
Combs and surfaces cleaned and disinfected
checklist: Set up a private, well-lit consultation area and seated the client comfortably
Used open questions and covered hair care, chemical history, health and allergies
Listened well, repeated back and noticed the client's body language
Checked the whole scalp in sections for flakes, oil, sores, infection or lice
Carried out porosity, elasticity and pull tests correctly and recorded the results
Noted texture, density, curl pattern and edge condition accurately
Identified any contraindication and explained the referral kindly, without diagnosing
Agreed a suitable service plan and aftercare and completed the record card
safety: Do not continue if you see signs of infection or lice; stop and tell the assessor
Wash hands before and after, and disinfect combs between clients
Pull gently in the pull test and elasticity test, and stop if the client feels pain
Keep each partner's health details private

practical2.title: Hair and scalp conditions chart and referral role plays
practical2.brief: As a group, make a large reference chart of hair and scalp conditions using your own drawings and the Centre's textbook pictures. Each member takes two or three conditions and writes the signs, whether it is infectious, and the salon action (work on it, change the service, or refer). Include dandruff, seborrhoea, psoriasis, ringworm, impetigo, head lice, folliculitis, alopecia areata, traction alopecia, split ends and trichorrhexis nodosa. Then act out three short role plays, with each member taking a turn as stylist, client or observer: (1) a client with signs of head lice; (2) a client with thinning edges from tight braids; (3) a client with dry, porous natural hair who wants a relaxer today. In each, the stylist uses open questions, explains in plain words, refers or changes the plan, and fills in a record card. The observer writes notes on what went well. Photograph each stage and hand in the chart, notes and record cards.
materials: Large poster paper or card, markers and rulers
Textbook pictures of hair and scalp conditions
Client record cards and observer note sheets
Pens, a table and two chairs for the role plays
photos: Each member working on their part of the chart
Role play 1 in progress, with the record card
Role play 2 in progress, with the record card
Role play 3 in progress, with the record card
The observer notes and record cards laid out together
checklist: Wrote correct signs for their conditions on the chart
Correctly said whether each condition is infectious
Gave the correct salon action, with referral where needed
As stylist, used open questions and listened well
Explained the problem in plain, kind words, in private, without a firm diagnosis
Changed the plan or referred correctly in each role play
Completed a clear record card for their role play
As observer, wrote useful notes on what went well and what to improve
safety: Role plays use no real chemicals or tools
Do not use real clients' names or health details
Keep the role-play area clear so nobody trips
Treat each other with respect during the role plays
